summary: Describes how an IS-IS system can originate more than 256 link state PDU fragments, a limit in the original protocol. It works for IP-only, OSI-only and dual routers. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 5311.

plainLanguage.summary: A router could only send its map in 256 pieces. This shows how to send more pieces when the map is big.

questions: how does is-is handle more than 256 lsp fragments
what is the is alias id tlv
how do mode 1 and mode 2 differ in lsp extension
subtitle: Workaround to extend IS-IS routing to support more than 256 link-state fragments.

tldr.problem: IS-IS routing protocol limits each router to 256 link-state PDU (LSP) fragments. Modern networks with multiple address families (IPv4, IPv6, OSI), traffic engineering, and many external routes exceed this limit, making it impossible for large routers to advertise all their information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3786 allows a router to advertise extra LSP fragments using additional "virtual" system IDs. An IS Alias ID TLV in each fragment links the virtual LSPs back to the router's real system ID, and two operation modes allow either backward-compatible or unrestricted advertising.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was replaced by RFC 5311, which provides a more comprehensive solution to the LSP fragmentation problem.

today: RFC 3786 is Informational and was superseded by RFC 5311, which provides a more comprehensive approach to the LSP fragmentation problem in IS-IS. Large routers in modern networks continue to use extension mechanisms to advertise more than 256 LSP fragments when necessary.

sections.title: The 256 LSP Fragment Limit
sections.content:
In IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) routing, routers flood their link-state information in units called Link State PDUs (LSPs). These logical LSPs can become very large, so the protocol fragments them. The original IS-IS specification (ISO/IEC 10589) limits each router to 256 fragments.

With modern networks, the limit is increasingly exceeded. Factors contributing include: new TLVs and sub-TLVs carrying traffic engineering data, separate address families (IPv4, IPv6, OSI), growing numbers of external routes injected into areas, finer-granularity routing, and optical network information. Large router architectures run out of fragment space, unable to advertise all their links and adjacencies.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a router's network map is split into 256 pages. But with modern networks having lots of links, addresses, and special routing info, you need more pages. The problem is the IS-IS rule says "stop at 256 pages."

sections.title: The Virtual System ID Solution
sections.content:
The solution uses additional system IDs assigned by the network administrator. Each additional system ID allows a router to generate 256 more LSP fragments. A router advertises the extra information as if multiple "virtual" routers are originating it, even though one physical router controls all of them.

A new IS Alias ID TLV (Type Length Value) in each LSP fragment links the virtual LSPs back to the router's real system ID. Extension-capable routers recognize this link and combine the original and extended LSPs for routing computation, treating them as one logical LSP. This allows the router to exceed the 256-fragment limit while remaining compatible with non-extension-capable routers that treat each system ID as a separate router.
sections.plainLanguage: If one router has system ID 'A' and needs more than 256 pages, it pretends to be routers 'B' and 'C' also, each sending 256 pages. It includes a special note in each page saying "pages labeled B are actually from router A, and pages labeled C are also from router A." New routers understand the note and combine them; old routers think B and C are separate routers.

sections.title: Two Operation Modes
sections.content:
Operation Mode 1 prioritizes backward compatibility. Extended LSPs can only carry "leaf" information (addresses and services that are destinations, not transit points). The originating router advertises zero-cost adjacencies from itself to each virtual system, making virtual systems appear as stubs reachable only through the original router. This means older routers, which do not understand the extension, can still correctly interpret the network topology.

Operation Mode 2 removes the leaf-only restriction and allows any link-state information in extended LSPs. However, it changes how LSPs are processed in the Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm in a way that is incompatible with older implementations. Mode 2 requires that all routers in the area support the extension.

Routers may run different modes on different levels (Level 1 vs. Level 2) or areas. The RFC recommends Mode 2 when all routers support the extension, since it is more flexible. Mode 1 is only necessary to interoperate with older, non-extension-capable routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Mode 1 is safe with old routers: fake routers only advertise addresses, not connections to other routers, so old routers understand the topology correctly. Mode 2 is faster but all routers must understand the trick. You pick the mode that matches your network's age and capabilities.

sections.title: IS Alias ID TLV and LSP Handling
sections.content:
Each LSP in fragment 0 carries an IS Alias ID TLV containing the router's real system ID and pseudonode number. This 8-octet structure (6 octets for system ID, 1 for pseudonode, 1 for sub-TLVs length) ties all fragments of the same logical router together.

When generating LSPs, a router treats extended LSPs like original LSPs, with a few exceptions: the Attached (ATT) bits should be zero on extended LSPs (so older routers prefer the original LSP as the exit point), the Partition Repair (P) bit should be zero, and the overload bit should be consistent across all LSPs. LSP fragment 0 of each extended set must be generated to enable proper SPF processing.

For Mode 1, the originating router advertises the virtual system as a neighbor with metric zero, and the virtual system advertises back to the originating system with metric MaxLinkMetric - 1, satisfying the two-way connectivity check.
sections.plainLanguage: Each page carries a note saying "I belong to the real system ID." When processing, routers combine pages with the same note. Some flags on the pages differ slightly so old routers understand the fake routers can only be reached through the real one.

sections.title: Interoperability and Transition Strategy
sections.content:
For Mode 2, all routers in the area must be extension-capable. However, if extended information does not contain routing information (for example, optical-specific data carried by optical switches), older routers can safely ignore it.

A network can transition incrementally: first, upgrade routers one-by-one to run Mode 1. Non-extension-capable routers will interoperate correctly since Mode 1 LSPs appear as stubs. Then, when all routers are upgraded, configure them one-by-one to Mode 2.

The RFC recommends that implementations provide a configuration parameter to control extension behavior, with the default being disabled (standard IS-IS behavior). This prevents unexpected changes when software is upgraded.
sections.plainLanguage: You can add support one router at a time. Start with safe Mode 1 and old routers will still work. Once everything is upgraded, switch to Mode 2. This prevents confusion if software is upgraded without planning.
